Screened Electrification Equipment#

In brief. Electricity demand is growing faster than the grid can carry it. Regulated utilities pay for the new wires, transformers and substations; the equipment makers and contractors that supply them are paid as the work is delivered. The strategy ranks every electrification company on one score of fourteen measures (capital intensity, revenue growth and acceleration, earnings and revenue surprises, price trends and sensitivity to power markets), holds the best-scoring half of those suppliers and shorts the weakest fifth of electrification companies, today mostly the utilities and pipelines doing the paying.

The grid stress that took hold in 2023 looks durable. Utilities have committed to multi-year capital plans, equipment lead times run to years, and real yields remain elevated. The suppliers' own filings show no slowdown: their median revenue growth is 10.5% a year after inflation and still accelerating, the fastest since early 2023. Over that period the long/short has delivered a Sharpe ratio of 2.05 after trading costs, with a beta of 0.54 to the S&P 500. It steps aside into T-bills whenever real yields turn negative or suppliers' sales stop growing after inflation — the one environment in which it has failed.

Backtest window: January 2019 – August 2026 · All strategy figures are after trading costs (10bp on every trade) and borrow · Management fee not assumed

Sharpe uses a flat 4.0% risk-free rate. Returns are total returns, dividends reinvested. The strategy's figures are after 10bp on every trade — long and short name changes, resizing, sleeve and short resets, and each step-aside switch — and 1% a year borrow on the short (Costs); the "before trading costs" row removes the 10bp. ETF returns are net of their own fees. Max time under water is the longest stretch below a previous peak within the window; "+" means the drawdown was still unrecovered at the end of 2022.

This is a grid-tightness strategy. It does not work well when the grid has ample spare capacity: in 2020–21 the suppliers' median revenue growth fell to −8% a year after inflation, and the strategy trailed the theme ETFs. There is no exit signal for the buildout itself, but the strategy de-risks on its own. It steps aside into T-bills unless both the 10-year real yield and the suppliers' real revenue growth are above zero (the step-aside rule — it held T-bills from November 2019 to April 2022). Within the book, position size falls automatically as volatility rises or prices run far above trend (to a third of full size in April 2025), and the ranking rotates toward suppliers whose sales are still growing.

Since 2023 the strategy leads every benchmark on every measure but one — the S&P 500 recovered from the 2025 tariff selloff slightly faster (4.2 months under water against 4.4). Before 2023 it was a capital-preservation strategy: a quarter of the drawdown of the theme ETFs, the highest Calmar ratio, and almost no market exposure — but a lower Sharpe and return than GRID and PAVE, and a long spell under water (July 2019 – June 2022), most of it spent in T-bills while a clean-energy rally lifted exactly the stocks the rules exclude.

It fell through the COVID crash, then recovered and ended the spell about 25% above where the strategy stood in T-bills: the step-aside rule gave up return in 2020–21 in exchange for avoiding the swings.

Portfolio Construction#

The gap in capital intensity between the utilities and their suppliers is a fact in the accounts rather than a judgment call, which is what lets the whole portfolio be built by rule. The long book and the short side go through the same stages (screen, rank, weight) and are ranked on the same fourteen-signal score: the long book holds the top half of its screened suppliers, the short the bottom fifth of the wider universe. The long book adds risk control, and one rule decides when to step aside. The exact thresholds, timing and data behind every rule are in the rule book.

Aspect Long book Short book Source
SCREEN
 Electrification population Companies in the SEC's electrical-equipment and power industry codes, plus nuclear fuel-cycle names found by keyword; at least $10m of stock traded on a typical day over the past year and a full year of price history (about 200 names)
  • Industry codes: SEC EDGAR
  • Keywords: SEC EDGAR full-text search
  • Prices and volume: Yahoo Finance
On-theme The 10-K annual report used data center, substation, switchgear, transmission and distribution, grid modernization or electric utilities in the previous four years SEC EDGAR full-text search of 10-Ks
Supplier, not owner Capital spending ÷ sales in the lightest 60% of the population, which separates suppliers from the utilities that own the wires -- SEC EDGAR XBRL filings
Profitable Trailing-12-month net income above zero, using only figures already filed at the time -- SEC EDGAR XBRL filings
Not subsidy-dependent No 10-K in the previous four years mentions the investment tax credit, production tax credit, advanced manufacturing production credit or net energy metering -- SEC EDGAR full-text search of 10-Ks

  • From filings (6): capital intensity, revenue acceleration, revenue growth, revenue and earnings surprises, growth in capital spending
  • From prices (2): 12-month momentum, 1-month reversal

    • Congestion: mean absolute day-ahead congestion, PJM zones; benefits from a constrained grid
    • Scarcity: 99th-percentile hourly day-ahead price, ERCOT hub; benefits from price spikes
  • Average the fourteen standardised scores
  • Filings: SEC EDGAR XBRL filings
  • Prices: Yahoo Finance
  • Power: PJM and ERCOT day-ahead market prices
Selection Hold the top half each quarter; a held name stays while in the top 65% Short the bottom fifth, re-formed each quarter (16 names on average, never fewer than 12, 24 today) --
WEIGHT
 Equal weight Each name weighted equally Each name weighted equally; $0.25 short for every $1 of capital, reset each month --
RISK CONTROL
 Volatility target Size the book daily to target 20% annual volatility, never above 1.5×; resize only on moves of more than 20 points of exposure None of its own: the short stays at $0.25 per $1 of capital while these controls shrink the long side, so the book moves toward market-neutral as it de-risks --
Stretch de-lever Cut to 80% when the book is over 15% above its 200-day average or far ahead of the market; 60% at extremes --
Gold / Treasury sleeve 15% in GLD and IEF, reset monthly --

Step-Aside Rule#

We hold the strategy only while the regime is green: the 10-year real yield is above zero and the suppliers' revenue is still growing after inflation. The first is the 10-year inflation-protected Treasury (TIPS) yield; the second is the median trailing-twelve-month revenue growth, as filed and less CPI inflation, of the names that pass the long-book screen. When either turns negative, the whole portfolio — long, short and sleeve — moves into 3-month T-bills the next day, and returns when both are positive again. See Real Yields and the Buildout.

The strategy beat GRID in every year from 2022 to 2025 and trails it so far in 2026, when the theme itself has rallied hard. It held T-bills from November 2019 to April 2022, so it missed GRID's 49% and 28% in 2020 and 2021 — a rally in the clean-energy and subsidy stocks the rules exclude — but also the COVID crash, and was up 4.5% in 2022, when the S&P lost 18%.

Over its one episode the step-aside rule cost return — it gave up 11 points in late 2019, 7 in 2020 and 22 in 2021, and saved 9 in 2022 — in exchange for holding the strategy flat through the COVID crash and the 2022 rate shock, which cut the worst drawdown from −13.9% to −11.1%.

Real Yields and the Buildout#

The step-aside rule exists because the strategy has one clear weakness: a market that no longer rewards what it holds. Two conditions mark that market, and the strategy stays invested only while both hold.

  • Real yields above zero. When the 10-year real yield is negative, money is effectively free, and the market pays up for distant earnings, subsidy-dependent growth and story stocks — everything the rules exclude. When it is positive, capital has a cost, and suppliers that are paid now are worth more than companies spending heavily to be paid later.
  • Suppliers' revenue still growing after inflation. When the median supplier's real sales are shrinking, the buildout is not reaching the companies the strategy owns, and the ranking has little to separate winners from losers.
Sharpe, full Sharpe, 2019–22 Sharpe, 2023 on max drawdown, full Calmar, full return a year time invested
Step-aside rule: both conditions (the strategy) 1.34 0.44 2.05 −11.1% 1.88 20.8% 67%
Real yield alone 1.30 0.39 2.05 −11.1% 1.87 20.6% 70%
Always invested 1.38 0.79 2.05 −13.9% 1.80 25.1% 100%
  • It costs nothing in the grid-tight period. Both conditions have held since spring 2022, so the step-aside rule has not been triggered since; every 2023-on figure is identical with or without it.
  • It trades return for protection when the environment turns. Over the full period the worst fall drops from −13.9% to −11.1% and the Calmar ratio edges up (1.81 to 1.88), but return is about 4 points a year lower and the Sharpe ratio slightly lower (1.34 against 1.38): the long book did well in 2020–21, the years the rule spent in T-bills. The dashed line in the rolling-Sharpe chart shows what it stepped around.
  • Requiring both conditions performs about the same as real yields alone (Sharpe 1.34 against 1.31) and steps aside a few months earlier — in November 2019, as supplier sales began to shrink, rather than in March 2020. We use both because each describes a different half of the thesis: the cost of capital and the buildout itself.
  • Rising real yields also help the short. Utilities trade like bonds: their monthly returns move against changes in the real yield (correlation −0.4 to −0.7 in every period since 2013), and they fell 2–3% on average in months when real yields jumped more than 0.2 points.
  • Where it stands now. The 10-year real yield was 2.44% at the end of August 2026, close to its post-2008 high of about 2.5%, and suppliers' real revenue growth is 10.5% and rising. Both conditions are well clear of triggering.

The caveat. The rule has been tested on essentially one episode — late 2019 to spring 2022 — and it was designed after seeing that episode. We adopt it because the mechanism is clear and the weakness is known, not because the backtest proves it; it will be judged on the live record. Its case rests on limiting drawdowns, not on raising the Sharpe ratio: staying invested throughout would have earned more, with a deeper worst fall. Moving to T-bills also lengthens recovery: the strategy's July 2019 peak was not regained until June 2022.

Return Attribution#

A regression of each book's daily return on GRID's (or the S&P's): whatever is left after accounting for exposure to the theme is alpha. A t-statistic above 2 means the result is unlikely to be luck.

2023 – Aug 2026 alpha a year t-statistic
Long/short vs GRID 21.7% 3.9
Long/short vs S&P 500 20.8% 3.4
Ranking alone: top half vs all qualifying names, equally weighted 7.1% 2.7
  • The alpha survives the short. About 21.7% a year against GRID since 2023, at a beta of 0.47 to GRID: the short removes theme exposure, not stock-selection skill.
  • The alpha is statistically strong, with a t-statistic of 3.9 against GRID and 3.4 against the S&P 500.
  • The ranking adds about 7 points a year over holding every qualifying name equally (t ≈ 2.7). Much of that shows up together with the volatility target: the ranked names are more volatile, and the target sizes them down when they are. It reflects how the ranking and the risk controls work together, not stock picking alone.

Style Factors#

The alpha above could in principle be a disguised bet on well-known investment styles. To check, the same regression was re-run with style factors added alongside GRID.

2023 – Aug 2026, controlling for alpha a year t-statistic
GRID only (as above) 21.7% 3.9
Academic factors 18.7% 3.6
Academic factors + GRID 18.6% 3.8
ETF style factors + GRID 22.8% 4.6

Academic factors (daily, Kenneth French data library): the five Fama-French factors (market, size, value, profitability and investment) plus Carhart momentum.

ETF style factors (each measured as the gap between two ETFs):

style measured as
Momentum MTUM (iShares MSCI USA Momentum) minus SPY
Growth vs value IWF (Russell 1000 Growth) minus IWD (Russell 1000 Value)
Quality QUAL (iShares MSCI USA Quality) minus SPY
Low volatility USMV (iShares MSCI USA Min Vol) minus SPY
Size IWM (Russell 2000) minus SPY
  • What the styles explain: about 3 points of the 21.7%. Over the full 2019–2026 period the alpha is 12–15% a year, with t-statistics of 3.3–4.1.
  • The book does lean on some styles:
  • Momentum: clearly positive (a loading of 0.23–0.32, meaning the book tends to move about a quarter to a third as much as the momentum factor). This is the one that matters: if momentum stocks sell off sharply, the strategy will likely fall with them (see Momentum Sell-Offs below).
  • Small size and profitability/quality: moderate tilts. That fits the rules, which pick profitable, capital-light mid-caps.
  • Growth vs value: a slight tilt toward growth on the ETF measure (0.13) and none on the academic value factor, so it isn't a disguised growth bet.
  • Low volatility: it leans away from low-volatility stocks.
  • Most of the return is not style: the factors explain only about half of the daily variation (R² 0.49–0.54).

Episodes are peak-to-trough falls of at least 7% in the Fama-French momentum factor, plus July 2024 (when the MTUM ETF fell 13%) and the DeepSeek day (a shock to the AI-power theme). The strategy held T-bills from November 2019 to April 2022 under the step-aside rule.   • Momentum sell-offs come in two kinds. In most of them (2019, 2020–21, mid-2022, early 2023) momentum fell because beaten-down stocks rebounded in a rising market. The strategy stayed positive every time it was invested but lagged GRID, PAVE and the S&P 500, because its low beta and the short side cap its upside. Had the step-aside rule kept it invested through 2020–21, it would still have made money in all three of that period's crashes (0.8% to 6.1%), though far behind GRID and PAVE.
  • In sell-offs in a falling market it generally lost less than GRID: −1.4% against −8.9% in July 2024 and −6.5% against −9.3% in June–August 2026, level on the DeepSeek day (−5.6%), but slightly more in February–March 2025 (−6.2% against −5.5%).
  • Its largest loss in any episode is −6.5%, in the one still under way at the end of the data.

Short Book Detail#

Short Basket Composition#

The shorted stocks rose 6.4% a year over the full period, against 20.8% for PAVE, with a worst fall of −47%. They move with the theme, so the short gains when the theme falls and cushions the long book. They have also risen far less than the theme, so in a rising market the short costs much less than the long book earns.

Rationale for the Short#

As is desirable of short legs, the short doesn't need its member names to fall but only to do worse than the long book. The proposed strategy accomplishes this. The long book has beaten the shorted stocks in both rising and falling months (by 3.5% a month when GRID fell and 1.4% when it rose).

2023 – Aug 2026, average month shorted stocks long book long book − 0.25 × shorted stocks GRID
GRID down (17 months) −4.5% −1.1% 0.1% −3.8%
GRID up (27 months) 4.0% 5.4% 4.4% 5.5%
All months (44) 0.7% 2.9% 2.7% 1.9%

Long book: the long side with its risk controls, before the short. Best in each row in bold, between the last two columns.

The short costs about 3 points of return a year (39.5% to 36.8% since 2023), and in exchange cuts the worst drawdown from −17.2% to −10.2% and beta to the S&P 500 from 0.76 to 0.54, raising the Sharpe ratio from 1.87 to 2.05. In months when GRID fell, the strategy was close to flat.

It is weakest when beaten-down stocks rebound sharply. The shorted stocks are largely recent laggards, so when laggards rally, as in mid-2020 and mid-2022, they rose 25–36% in a few weeks and the short cost money. In falling-market sell-offs it helped: in February–March 2025 the shorted stocks fell 11.6% and the short cut the book's loss from −8.9% to −6.2%.

About half the basket, on average since 2019, is utilities, power producers and pipelines — the companies paying for the buildout. The rest are electrification industrials that the buildout is passing by.

PAVE Alternative#

PAVE is the simple alternative. A $0.25 short of the PAVE ETF (US infrastructure and electrical companies — closest in make-up to the long book) gives almost the same result under the same rules: Sharpe 1.24 over the full period and 2.00 since 2023, with a worst fall of −11.7% against −11.1%. It is one liquid line ($13.5bn fund, about $82m traded a day, listed options), normally cheap to borrow — no single-name borrow to arrange. We prefer the single-name short because its edge is in stock selection rather than index tracking; an investor who values simplicity gives up very little with PAVE.

Turnover measures how much is traded in a year relative to the portfolio's capital. Two-way counts every purchase and every sale: each day, the absolute change in every position's weight is added up, and the daily sums are totalled and annualised. One-way — the convention in fund prospectuses, including the ETF figures above — counts roughly one side, the lesser of purchases or sales, so it is about half the two-way figure. On the one-way convention the strategy trades like an active fundamental long/short fund or a systematic factor fund (typically 100–600% a year), not like an index ETF.
